A parabola is a smooth, curved line that is shaped like the letter U (or an upside-down U). It is perfectly symmetrical — if you draw a vertical line right down the middle of it, both sides are exact mirror images of each other. The curve never closes into a loop; it keeps opening outward and stretching on forever in both directions.

You have seen a parabola many times in real life without realizing it. The arc of a ball thrown through the air, the shape of a water fountain's stream, or the inner curve of a satellite dish — these are all parabolas (or very close to one).
The precise mathematical definition

Here is where things get wonderfully specific. A parabola is not just any U-shaped curve. It is defined with razor-sharp precision as:

The set of all points in a flat plane that are exactly the same distance from one fixed point as they are from one fixed straight line.

That fixed point is called the focus, and that fixed straight line is called the directrix.

Imagine you draw a straight horizontal line on a piece of paper — this is the directrix. Now place a dot somewhere above that line but not on it — this is the focus. Now ask yourself: which points on the paper are exactly the same distance from the dot as they are from the line? If you find all such points and connect them, you get a perfect parabola.

Every single point on the curve obeys this rule without exception. That is the heart of what a parabola is.
The key parts of a parabola

Vertex — This is the tip of the U, the single point where the curve turns around. It is the point on the parabola that is closest to both the focus and the directrix. The vertex sits exactly halfway between the focus and the directrix.

Axis of symmetry — This is the invisible straight line that passes through the focus and the vertex, dividing the parabola into two perfectly equal halves. It is the "backbone" of the parabola, and the curve is a mirror image on either side of it.

Focus — The special fixed point inside the curve. It lies on the axis of symmetry. The focus has a powerful geometric role: anything that travels parallel to the axis of symmetry and hits the curve gets redirected (reflected) directly toward the focus.

Directrix — The fixed straight line outside the curve, on the opposite side from the focus. It never touches or crosses the parabola. Its role is to define the shape in partnership with the focus — by saying that every point on the parabola is equidistant from both.

Latus rectum — This is a chord (a line segment connecting two points on the curve) that passes through the focus and is perpendicular to the axis of symmetry. Its length tells you how "wide" the parabola is at the level of the focus. The wider the latus rectum, the more open and flat the parabola; the narrower it is, the more pinched and steep.
How the focus-directrix distance shapes the parabola

The distance between the focus and the directrix controls everything about how the parabola looks. Specifically, the distance from the vertex to the focus (let's call it p) determines the shape:

  • If p is small (focus is very close to the directrix), the parabola is narrow and steep, like a tall thin U.
  • If p is large (focus is far from the directrix), the parabola is wide and flat, like a shallow bowl.

This single number p completely governs the curvature of the shape.
Which direction can a parabola open?

A parabola can open in any of four directions depending on the orientation of the axis of symmetry:

  • Upward (the classic U shape)
  • Downward (an upside-down U, like an arch)
  • To the right (a sideways C shape)
  • To the left (a reverse C shape)

In each case, the focus is always inside the curve (on the open side), and the directrix is always outside the curve (on the closed side, behind the vertex).
The parabola as a conic section

A parabola belongs to a famous family of curves called conic sections. These are the curves you get when you slice a cone with a flat plane at different angles.

Imagine a perfect geometric cone (like two ice cream cones placed tip-to-tip). If you slice through it:

  • At a slight tilt parallel to the slant edge of the cone — you get a parabola.
  • Straight across horizontally — you get a circle.
  • At an intermediate angle — you get an ellipse (an oval).
  • At a steep angle that cuts through both halves of the double cone — you get a hyperbola (two separate open curves).

The parabola is the boundary case between the ellipse (a closed curve) and the hyperbola (two open curves). It is the one conic section that has exactly one "branch," is open (not closed), and has an eccentricity of exactly 1. Eccentricity is a number that measures how stretched or open a conic section is — a circle has eccentricity 0, an ellipse is between 0 and 1, a parabola is exactly 1, and a hyperbola is greater than 1.
The equation of a parabola

In mathematics, a parabola is commonly expressed as an equation. The simplest standard forms are:

For a vertical parabola (opening up or down):
y = ax² + bx + c

or in a neater "vertex form":
y = a(x − h)² + k

where (h, k) is the vertex and a controls the direction and steepness. If a > 0, it opens upward. If a < 0, it opens downward. The larger the absolute value of a, the narrower the parabola.

For a horizontal parabola (opening left or right):
x = ay² + by + c

The most iconic and elementary parabola of all is simply y = x², which gives a symmetric U-shape with its vertex at the origin (0, 0).
The reflective property — the most powerful feature

This is one of the most remarkable things about a parabola, and it is the reason it appears in so much technology.

Any ray or beam traveling parallel to the axis of symmetry, when it strikes the inner surface of a parabola, reflects directly through the focus. Conversely, any ray or beam originating at the focus reflects off the parabola and travels outward perfectly parallel to the axis of symmetry.

This is not approximate — it is geometrically exact. And it has enormous practical implications:

  • Satellite dishes and radio telescopes are parabolic so that all incoming signals (which arrive as parallel waves from far away) are concentrated at the focus, where the receiver sits.
  • Car headlights and flashlights place a light bulb at the focus of a parabolic reflector so that the light bounces off and projects forward as a parallel, focused beam.
  • Reflecting telescopes (like the Hubble Space Telescope) use parabolic mirrors to focus incoming light to a point for observation.
  • Solar concentrators use parabolic troughs to direct sunlight onto a pipe at the focus to generate heat or electricity.
Where parabolas appear in the real world

Beyond technology, parabolas appear naturally and in design:

Projectile motion — When you throw a ball (ignoring air resistance), it travels in a parabolic arc. Gravity pulls it down at a constant rate while its horizontal speed stays constant, and the combination of those two motions traces a parabola.

Architecture — Parabolic arches appear in bridges and buildings because they distribute weight very efficiently. The Gateway Arch in St. Louis is sometimes compared to a parabola (though it is technically a catenary — see the next point).

Catenary vs. parabola — A chain hanging freely between two points forms a curve called a catenary, which looks very similar to a parabola but is mathematically different. However, a suspension bridge cable — which supports a uniform horizontal load (the road deck) rather than its own weight — actually does form a true parabola.

Parabolic microphones — The large dish microphones used at sports events are parabolic, collecting sound from a wide area and concentrating it at the focus where the microphone element sits.
How the parabola differs from curves it resembles

It is easy to confuse a parabola with other U-shaped curves, so it helps to know the distinctions:

A circle is a closed curve where every point is the same distance from a single center point. A parabola is open and infinite.

An ellipse is a stretched circle — a closed oval. A parabola is not closed.

A hyperbola has two open branches curving away from each other. A parabola has only one.

A catenary (the natural hanging-chain curve) looks like a parabola but is defined by a different equation (involving the hyperbolic cosine function, cosh x). The parabola grows as x², while the catenary grows slightly faster.
A one-sentence summary

A parabola is the precise U-shaped curve formed by all points that are equidistant from a single fixed point (the focus) and a fixed straight line (the directrix) — a geometrically exact shape with a perfect axis of symmetry, infinite arms, and a uniquely powerful reflective property that makes it indispensable in optics, engineering, physics, and architecture.
